items.content_excerpt: Nuvacore, a six-month-old semiconductor startup backed by Sequoia Capital, is seeking at least $200 million in funding at a proposed $2.5 billion valuation, Reuters reported. The round remains open, and the final terms could change. Based in San Jose, Nuvacore is developing a data-center CPU for AI workloads. Founded by semiconductor engineers Gerard Williams, John Bruno and Ram Srinivasan, the startup plans to design its processor’s core functionality before selecting an architecture, potentially differentiating itself from traditional x86 chips and existing Arm-based designs. It has yet to launch a product. Williams previously worked at Apple and founded Nuvia, acquired by Qualcomm for $1.4 billion in 2021. Meanwhile, Nvidia expects its Vera CPU to generate $20 billion in sales during its fiscal year ending in January, as AI systems increase demand for processors that coordinate specialized chips and autonomous agents. $NVDA

items.title: Microsoft is nearing a $4 trillion market capitalization for the first time in almost a year, marking a major recovery in investor confidenc
items.content_excerpt: Microsoft is nearing a $4 trillion market capitalization for the first time in almost a year, marking a major recovery in investor confidence and bringing the company close to its all-time valuation record. As of midday Friday, Microsoft was valued at $3.97 trillion, following a 2.38% gain in its shares. The company last surpassed the $4 trillion threshold on Oct. 29, 2025, after reaching a record market capitalization of $4.029 trillion the previous day, according to Dow Jones Market Data. The milestone underscores Microsoft’s renewed momentum after a volatile period in which investors reassessed its growth prospects, particularly its investments in artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Its ability to approach record territory again suggests that investors are regaining confidence in the company’s long-term position in the AI market and its capacity to translate technology investments into sustained business growth. $MSFT

items.title: @Triplsex @Murdangamez we've been focused on $IBM for a while, and IBM may still be a partner even if the impending announcement is anot
items.content_excerpt: @Triplsex @Murdangamez we've been focused on $IBM for a while, and IBM may still be a partner even if the impending announcement is another company. $MSFT invested in Fabrica over a decade ago - but that's also when Dagi was part of the team, and $GOOG belongs in the conversation as a dream partner. Or none of the above. One risk, even if it does turn out to be a dream partner, is that the contract value is not as exciting as hoped. These are interconnects, and the manufacturing platform to build them: we've seen other contracts for about $500K for single AME production setups, so how many would a hyperscaler need? Maybe it's just $2M for a couple machines to start warming up, and maybe up to $10M total over 5 years. That's not gonna send this into launch mode. Dagi buying more with what he can scrape together (looks like his monthly salary for the last month), and the fact that insiders have not filed any sales, continue to be the primary sources of confidence in continuing to hold.

items.title: Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position in Meta Platforms, arguing that alternative data from TickerTrends point to a significant slo
items.content_excerpt: Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position in Meta Platforms, arguing that alternative data from TickerTrends point to a significant slowdown in adoption of Muse, Meta’s flagship AI app, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg has highlighted as central to the company’s AI strategy. According to Hunterbrook Media’s report, weekly downloads fell 8.1% week over week to an average of approximately 165,000 per day during the seven days ended Oct. 7. Daily net additions of active users also declined sharply to around 74,000 in early October, down 62.4% from the average of 198,000 recorded in late September. Hunterbrook’s bearish thesis is that investor enthusiasm and Meta’s valuation gains may have outpaced the app’s actual operating performance. Beyond slowing user growth, the report identifies functional limitations, including access restrictions imposed by major third-party platforms such as Amazon, as well as increasing scrutiny over data privacy and security vulnerabilities. $META

items.content_excerpt: Silicon Valley’s AI boom is reshaping the tech industry as companies intensify their desperate hunt for computing power, specialized chips, infrastructure and top talent. Fierce competitors are increasingly forming unexpected alliances, while senior executives are personally stepping in to secure the resources needed to develop and deploy increasingly powerful AI models. The shortage of computing capacity has become a strategic bottleneck, forcing companies to rethink traditional partnerships and compete aggressively for the technology and expertise required to stay ahead. The battle for talent is equally intense. Google, eager to bring pioneering AI researcher Noam Shazeer back into its organization, paid $2.7 billion in 2024 to bring him back after he left to launch his own company. Shazeer returned to work on cutting-edge projects, including Gemini, Google's most advanced AI technology. $GOOGL

items.content_excerpt: $FLY What's going on behind the scenes at Firefly Thomas Zurbuchen, former NASA Science Chief, resigns from Firefly's board on September 30 with immediate effect, then shortly after joins Blue Origin in a senior executive role. Makes me wonder how long he'd been in discussions with Blue Origin. Both companies have serious lunar ambitions, but there's a big difference in resources. Blue Origin has Bezos backing it, while Firefly has to be much more selective with its capital. items.title: $TMUS T-Mobile's leadership didn't stay quiet; CTO John Saw published a direct, detailed public pushback titled "Spectrum Alone
items.content_excerpt: $TMUS T-Mobile's leadership didn't stay quiet; CTO John Saw published a direct, detailed public pushback titled "Spectrum Alone Doesn't Make a Network" to dismantle the panic narrative: The Divestment Fact: Saw pointed out that the 800 MHz spectrum SpaceX just bought from Grain is the exact narrow 14 MHz slice that T-Mobile willingly dumped and divested because it was no longer central to high-capacity 5G strategy. The Bandwidth Reality: Even after spending billions on Grain, Starlink Mobile commands only ~80 MHz of total spectrum (much of it uplink-only), while T-Mobile operates nearly 400 MHz of combined low- and mid-band spectrum. The Infrastructure Reality: Saw emphasized that owning spectrum is just the starting line—building a viable consumer carrier requires tens of thousands of cell towers, massive fiber backhaul, and ground infrastructure that satellites alone cannot replace. 2. AT&T Leadership Dismissal (John Stankey, CEO) AT&T CEO John Stankey addressed the development directly, calling the idea of SpaceX replacing incumbent cellular networks unrealistic: Technological Constraints: Pointed out that low-band satellite signals cannot handle dense urban data demands or penetrate heavy commercial structures without extensive ground femtocells and fiber feeds. Regulatory Hurdles: Stressed that transferring and repurposing spectrum for commercial terrestrial mobile use requires rigorous FCC approvals and interference studies, which will take years rather than months.

Buying the dip is the consensus trade. Just know you're betting the build stays slow, not that the threat is imaginary.

items.content_excerpt: $HUM +12.6% (436 at 12:25 ET), now above its old 52-week high of 428.88. The trigger is the 2027 Medicare star ratings: about 95% of Humana's MA members land in 4+ star plans for 2027, up from roughly 20% this year (per Reuters). JPM was expecting 60-70%. Evercore puts possible 2028 bonus payments around 4.8B USD. Screener flags since the open: Quick Momentum buy, Yearly Extremes buy, Volume Surge buy at ~4.9x avg volume (projected). Up ~120% over 6M, but still about -10% over 3Y, so this reads more like a recovery from the 2025 ratings hit than a brand-new story. The odd part: JPM estimates $UNH falls to ~67% from 81% and $CVS to ~70% from 84%, yet UNH is +1.7% and CVS only -0.8% today. Already priced in for them, or is nobody looking yet? No position.

items.content_excerpt: $SPCX $T $VZ $TMUS $TMUS no material impact until 2029.Buy the fking dip!! First, the market isn't pricing 2026 earnings, it's pricing the trajectory. SpaceX isn't just buying this 800 MHz, it already bought mid-band from EchoStar and is expected at the 2027 FCC auction. Shotwell has talked about building terrestrial infrastructure too, not just rural satellite fill-in. That's the option value investors are scared of. Second, the rural-first framing cuts both ways: rural is where the threat starts, but it's also the lowest-margin business the telcos have. If Starlink Mobile eventually works in cities, that's when it gets real — and that's a years-and-tens-of-billions build. slow network, rural first, telcos keep the cities for years. Buying the dip is the consensus trade. Just know you're betting the build stays slow, not that the threat is imaginary.

items.title: U.S. telecommunications stocks suffered their steepest one-day declines in more than a decade on Friday as investors reassessed the growing
items.content_excerpt: U.S. telecommunications stocks suffered their steepest one-day declines in more than a decade on Friday as investors reassessed the growing competitive threat from SpaceX. The selloff followed the company’s announcement that it was acquiring low-band spectrum in a deal intended to pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major U.S. wireless carrier. Elon Musk’s company is expanding beyond satellite internet and positioning itself to compete directly with established telecom operators by combining its satellite infrastructure with mobile connectivity. The announcement intensified concerns that SpaceX could disrupt the wireless market, putting pressure on traditional carriers’ subscriber growth, pricing power and long-term profitability. Verizon plunged 8.75%, AT&T fell 9.81%, and T-Mobile dropped 13.27%, marking an especially severe selloff for the sector. $SPCX $VZ $T $TMUS

$TMUS T-Mobile's leadership didn't stay quiet; CTO John Saw published a direct, detailed public pushback titled "Spectrum Alone Doesn't Make a Network" to dismantle the panic narrative: The Divestment Fact: Saw pointed out that the 800 MHz spectrum SpaceX just bought from Grain is the exact narrow 14 MHz slice that T-Mobile willingly dumped and divested because it was no longer central to high-capacity 5G strategy. The Bandwidth Reality: Even after spending billions on Grain, Starlink Mobile commands only ~80 MHz of total spectrum (much of it uplink-only), while T-Mobile operates nearly 400 MHz of combined low- and mid-band spectrum. The Infrastructure Reality: Saw emphasized that owning spectrum is just the starting line—building a viable consumer carrier requires tens of thousands of cell towers, massive fiber backhaul, and ground infrastructure that satellites alone cannot replace. 2. AT&T Leadership Dismissal (John Stankey, CEO) AT&T CEO John Stankey addressed the development directly, calling the idea of SpaceX replacing incumbent cellular networks unrealistic: Technological Constraints: Pointed out that low-band satellite signals cannot handle dense urban data demands or penetrate heavy commercial structures without extensive ground femtocells and fiber feeds. Regulatory Hurdles: Stressed that transferring and repurposing spectrum for commercial terrestrial mobile use requires rigorous FCC approvals and interference studies, which will take years rather than months.

Elon Musk’s company is expanding beyond satellite internet and positioning itself to compete directly with established telecom operators by combining its satellite infrastructure with mobile connectivity. The announcement intensified concerns that SpaceX could disrupt the wireless market, putting pressure on traditional carriers’ subscriber growth, pricing power and long-term profitability.
